abstract: Invasion graphs map community assembly by linking communities that contain stable equilibria through successful invasions. By design, they leave aside transient communities that arise when species arrive before a community settles. Transitory invasion graphs (TIGs) complement this framework by recording every observed community, stable or transient, weighted by its frequency. In 500 simulated competitive communities of 5 - 25 species, assembly expanded through many transient communities, then contracted onto a few attractors. Competition limited the expansion: stronger interactions produced fewer communities but more transitions among them. The contraction reflected the attractor type: stable-equilibrium communities settled on the endpoints predicted by invasion graphs, whereas cyclic and chaotic communities kept turning over, most often through communities away from those endpoints. Repeated invasion attempts also rescued species with negative invasion growth rates and occasionally displaced uninvadable equilibria. Together, invasion graphs and TIGs reveal both where assembly can end and what is observed along the way.
